hints: Checking every pair works but takes O(n²). Can you avoid looking at pairs?
For each number x, the partner you need is target − x.
A hash map from value to index lets you ask “have I seen the partner?” in O(1).
two-sum.approach: Scan once, keeping a map of value → index. For each element look up target − x; if present you are done, otherwise store x. Store after the lookup so an element never pairs with itself.

hints: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed.
Which data structure gives you last-in, first-out access?
valid-parentheses.approach: Push every opening bracket on a stack. For a closing bracket the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. The string is valid only if the stack is empty at the end.

hints: Negative numbers and numbers ending in 0 (except 0) can never be palindromes.
You do not need the whole reverse. Reversing half the digits is enough and avoids overflow.
palindrome-number.approach: Peel digits off the end into a reversed number until it is at least as large as what remains. Then the two halves match if they are equal, or equal after dropping the middle digit for odd lengths.

hints: Let best[i] be the largest sum of a subarray that ends exactly at index i.
best[i] is either nums[i] alone, or nums[i] added to best[i−1]. Which is larger?
maximum-subarray.approach: Kadane's algorithm: keep the best sum ending at the current element, cur = max(x, cur + x), and track the maximum cur seen. Restarting is better exactly when the running sum has gone negative.

hints: For a fixed selling day, which buying day is best?
It is the cheapest price seen before that day, and you can maintain it while scanning.
best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.approach: Scan once, tracking the minimum price so far. The best profit for selling today is price − minSoFar; keep the maximum over all days.

hints: To stand on step n you came from step n−1 or step n−2.
That is the Fibonacci recurrence. You only need the previous two values.
climbing-stairs.approach: ways(n) = ways(n−1) + ways(n−2) with ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2. Roll two variables forward instead of storing a table.

hints: Sorting puts equal values next to each other.
A hash set can detect a repeat the moment it appears, without sorting.
contains-duplicate.approach: Insert each element into a set; if it is already present, return true. If the loop finishes, all values are distinct.

hints: The array is sorted, so one comparison can discard half of the remaining range.
Keep lo and hi as inclusive bounds and loop while lo <= hi. Compute mid as lo + (hi − lo) / 2.
binary-search.approach: Compare the middle element with the target. If equal, return it; if the middle is smaller, search the right half, otherwise the left half. Stop when the range is empty and return −1.

hints: Think of a window [left, right] that never contains a repeated character.
When the new character is already inside the window, how far must left move?
Store the last index of each character so left can jump straight past the old occurrence.
longest-substring-without-repeating-char.approach: Sliding window with a map of last-seen indices. For each right, if its character was seen at or after left, set left to that index + 1. The answer is the largest right − left + 1.

hints: The product except self is (product of everything to the left) × (product of everything to the right).
Build the left products in one pass, then multiply in the right products in a second pass from the end.
product-of-array-except-self.approach: Fill the output with prefix products (product of elements before i). Then sweep from the right keeping a running suffix product and multiply it into each position. No division is needed and zeros are handled naturally.

hints: Let dp[a] be the fewest coins needed to make amount a.
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a − coin]) over every coin that fits. dp[0] = 0.
Use a value larger than any real answer to mean “impossible”.
coin-change.approach: Bottom-up dynamic programming over amounts 0..amount. For each amount try every coin and take the best of dp[a − coin] + 1. If dp[amount] is still the sentinel, the answer is −1.

hints: Overlaps are hard to spot in random order. What if the intervals were sorted?
After sorting by start, an interval either overlaps the last merged one or starts a new group.
merge-intervals.approach: Sort by start. Walk the intervals: if the current start is at most the last merged end, extend that end to the maximum of the two ends; otherwise append a new interval.

hints: Each connected group of land cells counts once, however large it is.
When you find unvisited land, flood the whole island so you never count it again.
Use an explicit stack or queue if a large all-land grid could overflow recursion.
number-of-islands.approach: Scan every cell. On unvisited land, increment the count and run a DFS/BFS that marks every connected land cell visited.

hints: Water above a bar is limited by the tallest bar on its left and the tallest on its right.
At each index the water is min(maxLeft, maxRight) − height.
Two pointers moving inward can track both maxima without extra arrays.
trapping-rain-water.approach: Keep left and right pointers with their running maxima. Always advance the side whose maximum is smaller, since that side's water level is already determined; add max − height at that pointer.

hints: Let dp[i][j] be the edit distance between the first i letters of word1 and the first j of word2.
If the letters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1]. Otherwise 1 + the best of insert, delete or replace.
The base cases are converting to or from the empty string.
edit-distance.approach: Fill a (m+1) × (n+1) table. dp[i][0] = i and dp[0][j] = j. For each cell take dp[i−1][j−1] on a match, or 1 + min(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]) on a mismatch.

hints: A hash map of counts works, but there is a constant-space trick.
What is x XOR x? What is x XOR 0? Does the order matter?
single-number.approach: XOR all elements together. Pairs cancel to 0 and XOR is commutative, so only the unpaired element remains.

hints: Counting occurrences with a map works. Can you do it with O(1) space?
If you cancel each occurrence of the candidate with a different value, the majority still survives.
majority-element.approach: Boyer–Moore voting: keep a candidate and a count. A matching element increments the count, a different one decrements it, and at zero the next element becomes the candidate. The guaranteed majority is what remains.

hints: You know exactly which numbers should be present: 0 through n.
What does the sum of 0..n equal, and how does the actual sum differ?
missing-number.approach: The expected sum is n(n+1)/2. Subtracting the actual sum leaves the missing number. XOR-ing all indices and values also works.

hints: Two strings are anagrams if every letter appears the same number of times in both.
Sorting both strings, or counting letters, makes that easy to compare.
valid-anagram.approach: Compare letter counts: count up for one string, count down for the other, and check that every count returns to zero (or simply compare the sorted strings).

hints: This is a binary search, but the answer is a position even when the target is absent.
When the loop ends, lo is the first index whose value is not smaller than the target.
search-insert-position.approach: Binary search for the first index where nums[i] >= target (a lower bound). That index is both the match position and the insertion point.

hints: The answer lies between 0 and x. The function y × y is monotonic.
Binary search for the largest y with y × y <= x, and use 64-bit arithmetic to avoid overflow.
sqrt-x.approach: Binary search on y in [0, x]. If y × y <= x remember y and go right, otherwise go left. Compare using y <= x / y or a 64-bit product to prevent overflow.

hints: Testing every number for divisibility is too slow for large n.
Instead of testing, cross out the multiples of each prime you find.
Crossing out can start at p × p because smaller multiples were removed by smaller primes.
count-primes.approach: Sieve of Eratosthenes: mark 0 and 1 as non-prime, and for each prime p up to √n mark p², p²+p, … as composite. The unmarked numbers below n are the primes.

hints: Compare the middle element with the rightmost element.
If mid is greater than the right end, the minimum must be strictly to the right of mid.
find-minimum-in-rotated-sorted-array.approach: Binary search: if nums[mid] > nums[hi] the rotation point is right of mid so set lo = mid + 1, otherwise the minimum is at mid or left of it so set hi = mid. When lo == hi it is the minimum.

hints: After splitting at mid, at least one half is always properly sorted.
Decide which half is sorted, then check whether the target lies inside that sorted range.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.approach: Binary search. If nums[lo] <= nums[mid] the left half is sorted: go left when the target is in [nums[lo], nums[mid]), else right. Otherwise the right half is sorted and the symmetric test applies.

hints: Start with the widest container. Which line should you move to have any chance of a larger area?
Moving the taller line can only reduce the height limit while shrinking the width, so move the shorter one.
container-with-most-water.approach: Two pointers at both ends. Record min(h[l], h[r]) × (r − l), then move the pointer at the shorter line inward. Every discarded pair is provably no better than one already considered.

hints: For each house you either rob it or skip it.
If you rob house i you add its value to the best total up to house i−2. If you skip it, you keep the best total up to i−1.
house-robber.approach: dp[i] = max(dp[i−1], dp[i−2] + nums[i]). Only the previous two values are needed, so use two variables.

hints: A simple DP: dp[i] is the longest increasing subsequence ending at i, found by looking at all earlier smaller values. That is O(n²).
To reach O(n log n), keep for each length the smallest possible tail value. This list stays sorted.
longest-increasing-subsequence.approach: Maintain a sorted array tails where tails[k] is the smallest tail of any increasing subsequence of length k+1. For each x, binary-search the first tail >= x and replace it (or append if none). The final length of tails is the answer.

hints: You do not need to track every path, only how far you can possibly get.
If you reach an index beyond your current furthest reach, you are stuck.
jump-game.approach: Greedy: keep far, the furthest index reachable so far. Walk the array; if i > far the end is unreachable, otherwise update far = max(far, i + nums[i]).

hints: The number of ways to reach a cell is the ways to reach the cell above plus the ways to reach the cell to its left.
Every path is a sequence of (m−1) downs and (n−1) rights in some order. How many orderings exist?
unique-paths.approach: Either fill a DP grid with paths[i][j] = paths[i−1][j] + paths[i][j−1], or count orderings directly with the binomial coefficient C(m+n−2, m−1).
unique-paths.time: O(m × n) for DP, O(min(m, n)) with the formula

hints: For each day you want the nearest later day that is warmer.
Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day. What order are their temperatures in?
daily-temperatures.approach: Monotonic stack of indices with decreasing temperatures. When today is warmer than the day on top, pop it and set its answer to the index difference. Push today afterwards.

hints: A subarray sum is the difference of two prefix sums.
At each position you want to know how many earlier prefix sums equal currentPrefix − k.
A hash map from prefix sum to its count answers that in O(1). Seed it with 0 → 1.
subarray-sum-equals-k.approach: Walk the array maintaining the running prefix sum. Add the number of earlier prefixes equal to prefix − k to the answer, then record the current prefix in the map.

hints: Sorting and indexing works in O(n log n). Can you avoid sorting everything?
A min-heap of size k always holds the k largest values seen so far. Its top is the answer.
kth-largest-element-in-an-array.approach: Push elements into a min-heap, popping whenever the size exceeds k. After processing all elements the heap root is the k-th largest. Quickselect achieves O(n) average time.

hints: Unlike sums, a very negative product can become the largest after multiplying by another negative.
Track both the maximum and the minimum product of a subarray ending at the current index.
maximum-product-subarray.approach: Maintain hi and lo, the largest and smallest products ending at the current element. For each x take the max and min of (x, hi × x, lo × x), and update the global best with hi.

hints: Every palindrome mirrors around a centre.
There are 2n − 1 centres: n single characters (odd length) and n − 1 gaps (even length).
longest-palindromic-substring-length.approach: For every centre expand outward while the characters match, recording the longest span. A DP over substrings or Manacher's algorithm are alternatives.

hints: Let best[i] be the minimum cost to stand on step i, where you may begin on step 0 or 1 for free.
You reached step i from i−1 or i−2, paying the cost of the step you left.
min-cost-climbing-stairs.approach: best[i] = min(best[i−1] + cost[i−1], best[i−2] + cost[i−2]) with best[0] = best[1] = 0. The answer is best[n], the position just beyond the last step. Two rolling variables suffice.

hints: Let dp[i][j] be the LCS length of the suffixes starting at i in text1 and j in text2.
If the characters match, extend the diagonal. If not, take the better of skipping one character from either string.
longest-common-subsequence.approach: dp[i][j] = dp[i+1][j+1] + 1 when text1[i] == text2[j], else max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j+1]). The answer is dp[0][0].
longest-common-subsequence.space: O(m × n), reducible to O(min(m, n))

hints: If the total is odd the answer is immediately false.
Otherwise this becomes: can some subset sum to total / 2? That is a 0/1 knapsack.
partition-equal-subset-sum.approach: Let target = total / 2 and track which sums are reachable. For each number update reachable sums from high to low (or use a bitset shift) so each element is used at most once. Answer true if target is reachable.

hints: The answer is always between 1 and n + 1, so values outside 1..n do not matter.
Use the array itself as a hash table: try to place value v at index v − 1.
first-missing-positive.approach: Cyclic placement: for each index swap nums[i] into its home slot nums[v−1] while 1 <= v <= n and the target slot differs. Then the first index i with nums[i] != i + 1 gives answer i + 1, or n + 1 if all match. A hash set is a simpler O(n)-space version.

hints: For each bar, find how far left and right it can extend while staying the shortest bar.
A stack of increasing heights finds those boundaries in a single pass.
largest-rectangle-in-histogram.approach: Monotonic stack of (start index, height). When a shorter bar arrives, pop taller bars and compute their area as height × (i − start); the popped bar's start carries over to the new bar. A final sentinel height of 0 flushes the stack.

hints: Trailing spaces are the only trap: the last word is not necessarily at the last index.
Walk backwards from the end and skip spaces first.
Then count characters until you hit another space or the start of the string.
length-of-last-word.approach: Scan from the right: skip any trailing spaces, then count consecutive non-space characters until a space or index 0. No splitting or extra memory is needed.

hints: Each value should appear min(count in A, count in B) times.
Count the occurrences in one array with a hash map.
Walk the other array; when a value still has a positive count, emit it and decrement. Sort the output at the end.
intersection-of-two-arrays-ii.approach: Build a frequency map of the first array, then iterate the second: if the map still holds a positive count for the value, add it to the result and decrement the count. Sort the result for the required ascending output. Alternatively sort both arrays and merge with two pointers using O(1) extra space.

hints: The answer can never exceed the number of papers n.
Sorting makes it easy to ask 'how many papers have at least c citations?'.
Avoid the sort: cap each citation at n and count into buckets, then scan from high to low accumulating papers.
h-index.approach: Counting sort: bucket[min(c, n)]++ for every citation. Scan h from n down to 0 keeping a running total of papers with at least h citations; the first h where the total is >= h is the answer. Sorting descending and finding the last index i with citations[i] >= i + 1 also works in O(n log n).

hints: Ignore everything that is not a letter or digit, and ignore case.
Use two pointers moving toward each other.
Skip non-alphanumeric characters on each side before comparing the lowercase characters.
valid-palindrome.approach: Place one pointer at each end. Advance the left pointer past non-alphanumeric characters and retreat the right pointer likewise, then compare the two characters case-insensitively. Any mismatch means false; if the pointers cross, it is a palindrome. No cleaned copy of the string is needed.

hints: Because the array is sorted, equal values are adjacent.
A value is new exactly when it differs from the previous kept value.
Keep a write index and only advance it when you meet a new value.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-array.approach: Two pointers: `write` marks the end of the distinct prefix, `read` scans. When nums[read] != nums[write - 1] copy it to nums[write] and increment write. The first `write` elements are the distinct values in order.

hints: Non-zero elements must keep their relative order.
Think of compacting the non-zero values to the front.
Keep a write index for the next non-zero slot, then fill the rest with zeros (or swap as you go).
move-zeroes.approach: Single pass with a write pointer: every non-zero value is copied to nums[write++]. Afterwards fill positions write..n-1 with zeros. Swapping nums[read] with nums[write] instead does it in one pass with fewer writes when zeros are rare.

hints: Brute force over triplets is O(n³); can fixing one number reduce the rest to a two-sum problem?
Sort the array so equal values are adjacent and two pointers can work.
Skip repeated values for the fixed element and for both pointers so each distinct triplet is counted once.
3sum-count.approach: Sort. For each index i (skipping values equal to the previous i), run two pointers lo = i + 1, hi = n - 1. If the sum is below zero move lo up, above zero move hi down, and on a hit count it and advance both pointers past duplicates. The sort gives the O(n log n) base and the double loop O(n²) overall.

hints: All numbers are positive, so extending a window only increases its sum.
That monotonic behaviour is what makes a sliding window valid.
Grow the right end until the sum reaches the target, then shrink from the left while it still does, recording the shortest length.
minimum-size-subarray-sum.approach: Sliding window with a running sum: add nums[right]; while sum >= target, update the best length with right - left + 1 and subtract nums[left++]. Each index enters and leaves the window once. Return 0 if the best length was never updated. (A prefix-sum + binary search variant gives O(n log n).)

hints: A window is valid if (window length − count of its most frequent letter) <= k.
Maintain letter counts for the current window.
You never need to shrink the recorded maximum: keep a running max frequency and slide the window by one when it becomes invalid.
longest-repeating-character-replacement.approach: Sliding window over uppercase letters. Track counts and `maxFreq`, the highest count seen in any window so far. After adding s[right], if (window size − maxFreq) > k, remove s[left] and move left once. The answer is the largest window size reached. Using a stale maxFreq is safe because the window only grows when a new maximum appears.

hints: A permutation of s1 is a substring of the same length with identical letter counts.
Compare letter-count arrays of size 26.
Slide a window of length |s1| over s2, updating counts by adding the new character and removing the old one.
permutation-in-string.approach: Count letters of s1. Slide a fixed window of length |s1| across s2, maintaining its counts incrementally. Track how many of the 26 letters currently match s1's count; when all 26 match, return true. Updating is O(1) per step so the whole scan is linear.

hints: The array is sorted, so you do not need a hash map.
Look at the sum of the smallest and largest remaining values.
If the sum is too small move the left pointer right; if too large move the right pointer left.
two-sum-ii-input-array-is-sorted.approach: Two pointers at both ends. If numbers[l] + numbers[r] equals the target, return l + 1 and r + 1 (1-based). If it is smaller, increment l; if larger, decrement r. Each step discards a value that can no longer be part of the answer, giving linear time and constant space.

hints: If Koko can finish at speed k, she can also finish at any speed above k.
That monotonic yes/no property is what binary search needs.
Search k between 1 and the largest pile; hours needed at speed k is the sum of ceil(pile / k).
koko-eating-bananas.approach: Binary search the answer. For a candidate speed k compute hours = Σ ceil(p / k). If hours <= h, k is feasible so try smaller; otherwise try larger. The search space is [1, max(piles)] so it takes O(log max) feasibility checks of O(n) each. Watch for integer overflow when summing hours.

hints: The capacity can never be below the heaviest package nor above the total weight.
If a capacity works, any larger capacity works too.
Binary search the capacity; to test one, greedily load packages in order and count the days used.
capacity-to-ship-packages.approach: Binary search on capacity in [max(weights), sum(weights)]. Feasibility check: simulate loading in order, starting a new day whenever the next package would overflow the ship. If days used <= D, the capacity works so search lower, otherwise higher.

hints: You only need to change where each node's next pointer points.
Keep track of the previous node as you walk forward.
Before overwriting node.next, save the original next node so you do not lose the rest of the list.
reverse-linked-list.approach: Iterative: prev = null, cur = head. While cur exists: save nxt = cur.next, set cur.next = prev, then prev = cur and cur = nxt. prev is the new head. The recursive form reverses the tail first and then makes head.next.next = head, using O(n) stack.

hints: Always the smaller of the two current heads goes next.
A dummy head node removes the special case for the first element.
When one list runs out, attach the remainder of the other directly.
merge-two-sorted-lists.approach: Create a dummy node and a tail pointer. While both lists are non-empty, link the smaller head to tail and advance that list. Finally link whichever list still has nodes. Return dummy.next. Nodes are reused, so no new nodes besides the dummy are allocated.

hints: You do not know the length up front.
Two pointers moving at different speeds meet your need.
Move one pointer two steps and the other one step; when the fast one reaches the end the slow one is in the middle.
middle-of-the-linked-list.approach: Fast and slow pointers: slow advances one node, fast two. When fast is null or has no next, slow is the middle; for an even length this lands on the second middle node as required.

hints: Comparing with a copy of the list in an array works but uses O(n) space.
Find the middle, then reverse the second half in place.
Compare the two halves node by node; optionally restore the list afterwards.
palindrome-linked-list.approach: Use fast/slow pointers to find the middle, reverse the second half, then walk both halves together comparing values. If every pair matches it is a palindrome. This is O(n) time and O(1) extra space; re-reverse the second half if the input must stay intact.

hints: Duplicates are adjacent because the list is sorted.
Compare each node with its next node.
If they are equal, skip the next node by pointing cur.next past it; otherwise advance.
remove-duplicates-from-sorted-list.approach: Walk with cur. While cur.next exists: if cur.next.val == cur.val set cur.next = cur.next.next, else cur = cur.next. Only the first node of each run is kept. No dummy is required because the head is never removed.

hints: Removing from the end is easier if you know where the end is relative to a pointer.
Keep two pointers exactly n nodes apart.
Start both at a dummy head; move the lead pointer n steps, then move both until the lead hits the last node. The trailing pointer is just before the node to delete.
remove-nth-node-from-end-of-list.approach: Dummy node before head so removing the first node is not special. Advance `fast` n steps, then advance `fast` and `slow` together until fast.next is null. slow.next is the target; set slow.next = slow.next.next. One pass.

hints: The digits are already stored least-significant first, which is the order you add in.
Carry the overflow to the next digit.
Keep looping while either list has nodes or a carry remains; treat a missing node as 0.
add-two-numbers.approach: Walk both lists together with a carry. sum = a + b + carry; append sum % 10 to the result and set carry = sum / 10. Continue until both lists are exhausted and carry is zero. A dummy head simplifies building the result.

hints: You must relink nodes, so the node before each pair matters.
Use a dummy node and a pointer `prev` to the node before the current pair.
For each pair a -> b, rewire prev -> b -> a -> next, then move prev to a.
swap-nodes-in-pairs.approach: With dummy -> head, while prev.next and prev.next.next exist let a = prev.next, b = a.next; set a.next = b.next, b.next = a, prev.next = b, then prev = a. The dummy also handles the new head.

hints: Build two chains: nodes at odd positions and nodes at even positions.
Remember where the even chain starts.
After the loop, link the end of the odd chain to the head of the even chain.
odd-even-linked-list.approach: Set odd = head, even = head.next, evenHead = even. While even and even.next exist: odd.next = even.next; odd = odd.next; even.next = odd.next; even = even.next. Finally odd.next = evenHead. Each node is touched once and nothing is allocated.

hints: Arrays are sorted with random access; for linked lists merge sort is the natural fit.
Split the list in the middle with fast/slow pointers.
Sort both halves recursively and merge them with the merge-two-sorted-lists routine.
sort-list.approach: Top-down merge sort: find the middle (stop slow before the second half), cut the list in two, recursively sort each half and merge. Recursion depth is O(log n). A bottom-up version that merges runs of size 1, 2, 4, … reaches O(1) extra space.

hints: The result interleaves the first half with the reversed second half.
Find the middle, reverse the second half.
Then merge the two halves alternately, taking one node from each.
reorder-list.approach: Three steps: (1) find the middle with fast/slow pointers and cut the list there, (2) reverse the second half, (3) weave the two lists: first.next = second, second.next = firstNext, and so on. All done by relinking nodes in place.

hints: First check whether k nodes are actually available; otherwise leave the tail alone.
Reverse exactly k nodes with the standard iterative reversal.
Reconnect: the previous group's tail must point to the new head of this group, and this group's old head (now its tail) to the next group.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.approach: Use a dummy and `groupPrev`. For each group, find the k-th node (stop if there are fewer than k). Reverse the k nodes between groupPrev and kth.next, then set groupPrev.next to kth, move groupPrev to the old group head (now the tail) and repeat.

hints: The depth of a tree is 1 plus the larger depth of its two subtrees.
An empty tree has depth 0.
Recursion is the shortest solution; a level-order BFS counting levels also works.
maximum-depth-of-binary-tree.approach: depth(node) = 0 if null else 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). Equivalent BFS: process level by level and count levels. Mind the recursion depth on skewed trees; use the BFS or an explicit stack if it is a concern.

hints: Inverting means swapping the left and right child of every node.
Do it for every node, in any traversal order.
Recursively invert the children and then swap them (or swap first, then recurse).
invert-binary-tree.approach: invert(node): if null return null; swap node.left and node.right after (or before) inverting both subtrees; return node. An iterative BFS with a queue does the same swap at every dequeued node.

hints: A tree is symmetric if its left subtree is a mirror of its right subtree.
Write a helper that compares two nodes at once.
Two nodes mirror each other if their values match, a.left mirrors b.right and a.right mirrors b.left.
symmetric-tree.approach: isMirror(a, b): both null is true; exactly one null or different values is false; otherwise isMirror(a.left, b.right) && isMirror(a.right, b.left). Start with isMirror(root.left, root.right). An iterative version pushes mirrored pairs on a queue.

hints: Compare two trees node by node in lock step.
Handle the null cases first.
Equal if both null, or both non-null with equal values and equal left and right subtrees.
same-tree.approach: same(p, q): if both null return true; if only one is null or values differ return false; else return same(p.left, q.left) && same(p.right, q.right). Structure and values must both match.

hints: The longest path through a node uses its deepest left chain plus its deepest right chain.
Compute heights bottom-up with DFS.
While returning the height, update a global best with leftHeight + rightHeight.
diameter-of-binary-tree.approach: DFS returns the height of each subtree (edges to the deepest leaf). At every node the longest path through it is left + right, so keep a running maximum. The answer is that maximum, which need not pass through the root. One traversal suffices.

hints: Inorder means left subtree, node, right subtree.
Recursion is trivial; try the iterative version with your own stack.
Push nodes while going left; pop to visit, then move to the right child.
binary-tree-inorder-traversal.approach: Iterative: cur = root, stack empty. While cur or stack non-empty: go as far left as possible pushing nodes; pop a node, record its value, set cur = node.right. For a BST this yields sorted order. Morris traversal achieves O(1) space by threading.

hints: A valid path must end at a leaf, not at any node.
Subtract the node value from the target as you go down.
At a leaf, check whether the remaining target equals the leaf's value.
path-sum.approach: hasPath(node, remaining): null is false; if node is a leaf return remaining == node.val; otherwise recurse on both children with remaining - node.val and OR the results.

hints: Balanced means every node's subtree heights differ by at most 1.
Computing height at each node separately is O(n²) on skewed trees.
Compute height and balance in the same DFS, returning a sentinel (such as -1) when a subtree is unbalanced.
balanced-binary-tree.approach: height(node) returns -1 if either child is unbalanced or their heights differ by more than 1, else 1 + max of the child heights. The tree is balanced if height(root) != -1. Each node is visited once.
